question: Can complex generative systems be made more data-efficient, reusable, and compositionally generalizable by representing a target distribution as products or mixtures of smaller learned factors, and what is required to sample from or discover those factors in practice?

key_findings.claim: The paper is best read as a position and synthesis article, not as a new unified compositional algorithm or a self-contained cross-domain empirical study.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly call it a position paper. Its central evidence is a small synthetic distribution illustration, a Maze2D comparison using the model of Janner et al., one numerical language result attributed to Du et al. 2023b, and an application gallery whose Figures 6-14 are adapted from or explicitly assigned to prior papers. Training protocols, seeds, uncertainty, and common cross-domain metrics are not supplied for the gallery, so those examples support plausibility and breadth rather than a new controlled benchmark.

key_findings.claim: The main statistical argument is conditional: a correct sparse factorization can replace learning an arbitrary high-dimensional joint with learning lower-dimensional marginals or conditionals, enabling unseen recombinations when every local configuration remains in distribution.
key_findings.evidence: For four K-valued variables, the paper contrasts an unrestricted O(K^4) joint with a product such as p(A)p(B)p(C,D). Figure 4 qualitatively shows two-factor product and mixture models covering their target more faithfully than one monolith; its caption says the monolith receives twice as much data as an individual factor. Figure 5 reports lower Maze2D dynamics error and faster denoising-loss reduction after replacing a joint trajectory distribution with local Markov factors, but the factorized implementation uses trajectory chunks of length 8 for architectural compatibility and no numerical table or uncertainty is given.

key_findings.claim: Probability products provide a common programming interface for new tasks, but the claimed zero-shot character depends on already having compatible factors and an effective inference procedure.
key_findings.evidence: The paper writes goal-directed planning as q(tau) proportional to a trajectory prior times a start-goal factor, manipulation as a product over constraint factors, hierarchical planning as the product of language, video, and action models, bounded-region image synthesis as a product over box-conditioned image factors, and video stylization as pretrained-video times style-model likelihood. These constructions need no new joint-task training in principle, but every example presupposes appropriate pretrained components over aligned variables and the ability to evaluate or sample their composed unnormalized density.

Section 5.1, intractable product normalization and sampling

key_findings.claim: The proposed discovery story extends the agenda beyond hand-written graphs, but its examples do not establish that maximum-likelihood factor discovery uniquely recovers semantic or causally correct components.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 maximizes the likelihood of a product of component models. Low-dimensional encoders yield object, lighting, or expression factors in image autoencoding; pairwise encoders yield spring or charge potentials in particle trajectories; and a weighted product/mixture-like construction separates five ImageNet classes. The demonstrations are adapted from Du et al. 2021, Comas et al. 2023, Liu et al. 2023, and Su et al. 2024. The paper supplies no identifiability theorem, intervention test, component-count selection rule, or quantitative semantic-recovery metric, and later acknowledges failure under spurious correlations.

key_findings.claim: The paper correctly separates algebraic composition from sampling correctness: products are easy to specify as energy sums, yet neither tokenwise autoregressive multiplication nor ordinary reverse diffusion generally samples the desired product.
key_findings.evidence: For autoregressive factors, the exact next-token conditional of the product requires marginalizing all future suffixes, so multiplying local next-token probabilities is not exact. For diffusion models, the product of noisy intermediate distributions is not the noised form of the clean product. The proposed continuous-domain route treats each noise level as an EBM, sums energies, and runs annealed importance sampling with multiple MCMC transitions at every level; discrete composition uses Gibbs sampling or one learned generator as a Metropolis-Hastings proposal. The text explicitly warns that directly applying the reverse process to a summed score does not sample the intended composed distribution.

Sections 5.2-5.3, annealed MCMC and discrete sampling

key_findings.claim: The printed Appendix A does not establish its advertised exact equivalence between a standard reverse-diffusion step and ULA.
key_findings.evidence: As printed, the reverse mean omits the standard DDPM 1/sqrt(alpha_t) prefactor; the stochastic term is beta_t times a standard normal even though the preceding sentence calls beta_t the variance; epsilon divided by sqrt(1-alpha_bar_t) is labeled the score grad p_t rather than minus grad log p_t; and ULA is also written using grad p_t instead of a log-density or energy gradient. These probability, score, energy, and variance inconsistencies make the claimed sqrt(2) noise correction and 1/sqrt(2) temperature statement non-derivable from the displayed equations without unstated corrections.

key_findings.claim: The most concrete language result is inherited and does not isolate architecture-level compositionality or establish a matched efficiency advantage.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports that combining outputs from five GPT-3.5 instances in language space obtains 58.0 plus or minus 2.8 percent on MATH versus 55.0 plus or minus 2.9 percent for GPT-4, citing Du et al. 2023b because proprietary logits prevent direct probability-product sampling. No API snapshot, token budget, total inference cost, prompt-equivalence audit, or same-base-model single-agent ablation is given here; it is therefore evidence for an output-aggregation system, not for exact product-of-language-model distributions.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not demonstrate that a complete composed system is computationally or environmentally cheaper at inference than a monolithic alternative.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion argues that each constituent is smaller and can be distributed across machines, but its own recommended continuous sampler evaluates several models and repeats MCMC transitions at every diffusion noise level, while the language example invokes five model instances. There is no end-to-end latency, energy, memory, carbon, or quality-matched cost measurement. Component-level savings therefore do not imply system-level efficiency, especially as factor count and sampler mixing time grow.

anchors.section: Repeated MCMC at each diffusion noise level

key_findings.claim: The paper itself identifies structure selection, factor weighting, spurious dependence, and theory as the agenda's unresolved core rather than implementation details.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion says current systems assume fixed prespecified composition and weights, learned decompositions assume a product of independent components, real data contains spurious correlations that can make existing algorithms fail, and compositional generalization still lacks a suitable theory. It proposes automatic graph and weight discovery, priors or active interventions, and explicit within-model compositional structure as future directions.

anchors.section: Discussion and Future Directions, stated limitations

method.core_idea: Treat complex generative systems as probabilistic programs or factor graphs: train or discover smaller distributions over local variables, reuse them as modular experts, and define a new target distribution by products, mixtures, inversion, or repeated symmetric factors rather than retraining one joint model.
method.mechanism: Specify lower-dimensional component likelihoods; combine normalized factors through an unnormalized product whose energy is the sum of component energies; for continuous diffusion components, traverse noise-indexed composite EBMs with annealed MCMC; for discrete components, use Gibbs or Metropolis-Hastings proposals; and optionally learn the components through factorized maximum likelihood with low-dimensional encoders or pairwise relational encoders.
assumptions: The target joint has sparse, repeated, or otherwise useful factor structure; omitted interactions are negligible or learnable.
Each factor is trained on enough locally in-distribution data, including every local configuration needed by the intended recombination.
Component models agree on variable semantics, coordinate systems, support, noise schedules, and likelihood or energy scale.
The product has non-negligible overlapping support and a finite normalizing constant.
A sufficiently mixing MCMC, Gibbs, or Metropolis-Hastings procedure is affordable in the dimensionality and modality of interest.
The number, scope, graph, and relative weights of factors are known or can be learned without collapsing, duplicating, or entangling factors.
Maximum likelihood under the chosen bottlenecks identifies components that are useful for recombination, not merely one of many observationally equivalent decompositions.
Using several smaller components and a more expensive sampler is cheaper overall than training or serving the relevant monolithic baseline at matched quality.
Results adapted from heterogeneous prior systems are representative enough to support the paper's common architectural thesis.

techniques.role: Defines a new task distribution by multiplying reusable constraint, prior, conditional, or modality factors.
Reduces statistical complexity when an arbitrary joint can be represented by lower-dimensional factors.
Tiles local transition models over a trajectory instead of modeling a full state-action sequence jointly.
Combines sentence- or bounding-box-conditioned image factors to request unseen multi-condition scenes.
Aggregates complete outputs from proprietary language models when logits needed for exact product sampling are unavailable.
Couples language, video, and action plans through a joint product for hierarchical decision making.
Uses multiple bottleneck encoders inside a product likelihood to separate objects or global image attributes.
Associates one latent-conditioned factor with each particle pair to recover and recombine interaction potentials.
Uses learned component weights to partition a mixed image distribution and recombine class factors.
Implements products, mixtures, and inversions as operations on unnormalized energy functions.
Samples a continuous product by running repeated MCMC transitions through a sequence of composite diffusion EBMs.
Samples discrete products either coordinatewise or with one learned model proposing moves accepted under remaining factors.
Suggests implementing ULA-like corrections with repeated fixed-noise reverse steps, although Appendix A's printed derivation is inconsistent.

evaluations.setting: Two synthetic two-dimensional targets, one a product and one a mixture of two simple factor distributions
evaluations.metric: Qualitative target coverage in Figure 4; no numerical divergence, held-out likelihood, seeds, or uncertainty
evaluations.result: The two-factor model visually matches the intended bars or ring more closely than the joint model
evaluations.baseline: A monolithic generator whose caption says it receives twice as much data as an individual factor, versus two separately trained factors

evaluations.setting: Maze2D trajectory generation with 4D state, 2D action, roughly 10,000 timesteps per episode, and factorized chunks of length 8
evaluations.metric: Dynamics error versus 10-100 agent episodes and denoising loss versus up to 10,000 training iterations
evaluations.result: The plotted factorized dynamics error stays near 0.12 while the monolithic curve falls from roughly 0.31 to 0.20; the factorized model also reaches a visibly lower denoising loss sooner, but the paper provides no table or uncertainty
evaluations.baseline: A single joint trajectory generator using the Janner et al. 2022 model family

evaluations.setting: MATH benchmark output aggregation reported from Du et al. 2023b
evaluations.result: Five GPT-3.5 instances are reported at 58.0 plus or minus 2.8 percent
evaluations.baseline: GPT-4 at 55.0 plus or minus 2.9 percent; API version, token budget, latency, and total cost are not matched in this paper

evaluations.setting: Planning, robotic constraints, hierarchical foundation-model planning, image tapestries, and video style adaptation
evaluations.metric: Task-specific qualitative demonstrations and cited prior-paper results; no unified metric in the reviewed paper
evaluations.result: The gallery shows that factor products can instantiate each application, but efficacy is delegated to Janner 2022, Ajay 2023, Du 2023a, Yang 2023a/b, and related work
evaluations.baseline: Heterogeneous prior-paper baselines rather than a common quality-, data-, or compute-matched monolithic system

evaluations.setting: Object, relational-potential, and five-class ImageNet component discovery
evaluations.metric: Visual semantic correspondence and recombination examples
evaluations.result: Learned components appear to isolate objects, lighting or expressions, spring/charge interactions, and source classes, then generate hybrid scenes or trajectories
evaluations.baseline: Figures adapted from Du 2021, Comas 2023, Liu 2023, and Su 2024; no new quantitative identifiability or intervention baseline

limitations: Author-stated: current compositions assume a fixed prespecified graph and per-model weights, limiting adaptation to new tasks.
Author-stated: factor discovery assumes naturally independent components and can fail when real training data contains spurious correlations.
Author-stated: theoretical characterization of compositional generalization for separately trained generative models remains open.

Reviewer-identified: most cross-domain demonstrations and the only language number are inherited from cited papers, so this position paper does not independently validate a single method across modalities.

Reviewer-identified: the O(K^4) illustration concerns an unrestricted discrete joint; a structured monolithic architecture can already encode factorization, sharing, equivariance, or conditional independence.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 4 lacks a numerical metric and fully explicit accounting of whether factor examples, total observations, optimizer steps, and parameters are matched.
Reviewer-identified: Maze2D has no run count, uncertainty, held-out split detail, parameter count, wall-clock cost, or table, and the length-8 factorized chunks change the modeling problem.
Reviewer-identified: product normalizers are generally intractable, and the recommended repeated MCMC at every diffusion noise level can erase inference-time efficiency gains.
Reviewer-identified: separate experts may have incompatible support, calibration, energy scale, variable definitions, or diffusion schedules; no interface contract or calibration method is proposed.
Reviewer-identified: semantic components are not identifiable from observational maximum likelihood alone, and no causal intervention or uniqueness test is provided.

Reviewer-identified: the five-GPT-3.5 versus GPT-4 MATH comparison is not matched for model snapshot, prompting, aggregate tokens, latency, or dollars and implements output aggregation rather than exact probability composition.
Reviewer-identified: claims of environmental friendliness and easy deployment are not supported by system-level energy, networking, memory, latency, or life-cycle measurements.

Reviewer-identified: Appendix A's reverse-diffusion/ULA equations contain score, sign, prefactor, and noise-scale inconsistencies, so its exact sampler and temperature conclusions are unreliable as printed.

Reviewer-identified: mixture, product-of-experts, inversion, spatial tiling, and sequential factor chains have materially different semantics and failure conditions, but the position thesis sometimes treats them as one general operation.
Reviewer-identified: no safety or robustness mechanism handles a malicious, misspecified, or suddenly updated factor in a decentralized multi-institution composition.
failure_modes: Disjoint or nearly disjoint component support makes the product zero almost everywhere, yielding rejection, vanishing gradients, or a tiny brittle mode.
An overconfident or badly scaled energy dominates the product, suppressing otherwise compatible factors and causing oversharp samples.
A missing interaction edge admits locally plausible but globally inconsistent samples; an unnecessary edge forfeits the claimed data-efficiency advantage.
Spurious correlations are learned as components, so recombining factors outside the observational support produces implausible or causally incorrect samples.
A direct sum of diffusion scores followed by ordinary reverse sampling converges to a biased distribution rather than the desired clean product.
Annealed Langevin, HMC, Gibbs, or Metropolis-Hastings chains fail to mix between product modes in high dimension within a practical compute budget.
Discrete coordinatewise Gibbs updates become trapped when valid changes require coordinated token edits; a learned proposal can be rejected almost always by another factor.
Unsupervised factor learning collapses several encoders onto one component, duplicates a factor, or returns entangled but likelihood-equivalent components.
Components trained by different institutions use incompatible tokenization, coordinate frames, data conventions, or noise levels despite nominally sharing variables.
Errors in an early text, video, or action-plan factor propagate through the hierarchical product and create no region of joint consistency.
The total latency and energy scale roughly with the number of active experts times MCMC transitions, making the modular system slower or costlier than a monolith.
Factors are each locally out of distribution in a novel task even though their labels appear familiar, invalidating the locality premise behind recombination.
A discovered class or object factor changes meaning across datasets, so cross-model multiplication blends incompatible semantics rather than composing them.
reusable_insights: Separate the specification of a composed density from the algorithm that samples it; algebraically correct energy addition does not certify a correct reverse-diffusion sampler.
Evaluate a modular system at matched total data, parameters, optimizer work, inference evaluations, latency, energy, and quality, not only per-component size.
Treat factor interfaces as typed contracts covering variables, support, units, calibration, coordinate frames, likelihood scale, and noise schedule.
Stress-test products by measuring support overlap, effective sample size, chain mixing, condition satisfaction for every factor, and global coherence.
Use interventions or held-out recombination matrices to distinguish semantic factor recovery from observationally equivalent decompositions.
Report a structure-selection curve: quality and data efficiency versus missing edges, extra edges, factor count, and learned weights.
A strong benchmark should withhold combinations while keeping each local factor in distribution, then separately test cases where one or more local factors are also novel.
Products, mixtures, sequential chains, and spatial tiling should be benchmarked and documented as distinct composition operators.
For proprietary language models, output-space debate or aggregation is a useful modular system pattern but should not be described as exact likelihood multiplication.
Compositional modeling can be valuable even without net compute savings when modular substitution, auditability, or decentralized ownership is the primary objective.
Validate sampler derivations dimensionally and against a tractable Gaussian product before attributing failures to model quality or composition structure.
open_questions: Can graph structure, factor scope, and time- or state-dependent weights be learned jointly while remaining identifiable and computationally tractable?
What necessary and sufficient conditions on support, dependence, and score geometry make diffusion-model composition projectively correct?

Which sampler gives the best quality-cost tradeoff as the number of continuous or discrete experts grows: annealed MCMC, corrected reverse diffusion, sequential Monte Carlo, message passing, or amortized distillation?
Can a composed sampler expose a calibrated certificate that every local constraint and the global task distribution are simultaneously satisfied?
How should one measure compositional generalization separately from memorization, interpolation, ordinary OOD robustness, and increased test-time compute?
When does a single structured model with parameter sharing dominate separately trained factors in sample efficiency or compute?
Can active interventions recover causal components when observational data has strong spurious correlations?
How stable are discovered object, relation, or class factors across seeds, datasets, architectures, and component counts?
Can several proprietary autoregressive models be composed with black-box sampling while retaining an explicit target distribution and convergence guarantees?
What end-to-end latency, energy, network, fault-tolerance, and security costs arise in the decentralized daemon-style architecture?
How can newly updated or adversarial factors be sandboxed so that local modularity does not create global distribution failure?
After correcting Appendix A, how large is the bias of the proposed repeated-reverse-step approximation on analytically tractable products and modern high-dimensional models?

competitive_landscape.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: Compositional Generation with Energy-Based Diffusion Models and MCMC
competitive_landscape.difference: Du et al. isolate the sampler failure caused by composing noisy diffusion distributions, introduce energy-parameterized diffusion models and MCMC or Metropolis-corrected samplers, and evaluate them directly. The reviewed paper imports this core sampling machinery and broadens it into a cross-domain position; it does not supersede the predecessor experimentally.

competitive_landscape.title: Compositional Image Decomposition with Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Su et al. provide the concrete Decomp Diffusion method that infers several diffusion components from a single image and recombines local and global scene factors, including across models. Figure 12 in the reviewed paper is adapted from this work; the reviewed paper generalizes the lesson but supplies no stronger identifiability or decomposition evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Mechanisms of Projective Composition of Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Bradley et al. define a precise success criterion called projective composition, prove when linear score combinations and reverse diffusion can achieve it, identify failure conditions, and give a predictive heuristic. This directly fills the reviewed paper's acknowledged lack of theory and makes its broad claim testable rather than relying on a gallery of successes.

competitive_landscape.title: Composition and Control with Distilled Energy Diffusion Models and Sequential Monte Carlo
competitive_landscape.difference: Thornton et al. distill stable energy functions from pretrained score models and formulate diffusion sampling as a Feynman-Kac model controlled by energy potentials, enabling composition and low-temperature generation with sequential Monte Carlo. It targets the exact energy-training and MCMC scalability limitations that the reviewed paper leaves open.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Compositional Generation with Diffusion Models Using Lift Scores
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu and Gao use lift scores approximated from the original diffusion model to test each condition and resample toward joint satisfaction, with experiments on synthetic data, CLEVR spatial tasks, and text-to-image generation. The approach supplies an explicit per-condition learning-signal check and avoids separately training every energy factor, while still paying inference-time resampling cost.

competitive_landscape.title: How Compositional Generalization and Creativity Improve as Diffusion Models are Trained
competitive_landscape.difference: Favero et al. show theoretically and empirically that one diffusion model can learn hierarchical composition rules through context-based feature clustering, with polynomial context-size sample complexity and progressively growing coherence length. This complicates the reviewed paper's monolith-versus-modules framing: explicit separate experts are one route, not the only route, to compositional structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Factor Chaining: Coordinated Manipulation with Diffusion-based Factor Graph
competitive_landscape.difference: Mishra et al. instantiate modular diffusion factors as spatial and temporal edges in a planning graph and compose them with bidirectional message passing for unseen bimanual manipulation tasks. It is a narrower but more operational test of the reviewed paper's planning thesis, with an explicit graph and inference algorithm rather than a generic probability-product recipe.

competitive_landscape.title: From Global to Factor-Wise Expert Composition in Discrete Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: FactorDiff routes individual spatial or functional factors to the relevant discrete-diffusion expert instead of assigning one global scalar weight per sample, and evaluates the approach on ARC-AGI. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's request for learned structure and weighting, although only in a narrower discrete, factorized setting.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Complex generative systems should be built by composing smaller models because factorization can reduce data requirements, extrapolate to unseen combinations, program new task distributions without joint-task training, and expose discoverable and interpretable components.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines a discrete sample-complexity illustration, simple product/mixture and Maze2D demonstrations, a cited five-agent language result, a broad catalogue of cited planning and generation systems, three cited component-discovery mechanisms, and a practical survey of EBM, diffusion, MCMC, Gibbs, and Metropolis-Hastings composition.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Its meaningful novelty is conceptual integration: it turns probabilistic graphical-model factorization, product-of-experts energy arithmetic, diffusion composition, modular planning, and unsupervised factor discovery into one explicit research agenda opposing monolithic-only scaling. The paper's algorithmic novelty is limited because nearly every substantive application and the core sampler are prior cited results, and its few fresh illustrations lack a reproducible experimental section. By 2025-26, projective-composition theory, distilled-energy SMC, lift-score validation, factor-graph planning, single-model hierarchy theory, and factor-wise routing have made several of its open directions concrete. The strongest lasting contribution is therefore the abstraction and agenda, not proof that modular systems are universally cheaper, more accurate, or semantically identifiable.

reviewer_notes: All 12 cached pages were read, including the full references and Appendix A. Figures 3-14 and the appendix equations were rendered from the hash-pinned PDF to inspect axes, attribution captions, and mathematical notation; approximate Maze2D values above are visual readings because the paper gives no table. The PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 hashes exactly match the fulltext index, which reports all 12 pages with text. Eight adjacent or competing works were checked on official PMLR proceedings pages on 2026-08-23, spanning direct predecessors and 2024-26 follow-ups in sampling correctness, energy distillation, component discovery, condition validation, theory, robotics, and dynamic routing. This is a primary full-text review, not a reproduction of experiments or an independent audit of the cited systems' code and datasets.
